meta.blurb: Maya burns her toast while checking her phone, then realises she remembers nothing of the bus ride. A Thursday evening class in the community hall gives her six weeks of small, honest practice for being where she actually is.
meta.bible: Maya Ellis: a busy office worker of about thirty, always rushing and checking her phone. Mrs Adeyemi: the calm, kind teacher of the Thursday evening class at the Community hall. Joe: Maya's colleague, friendly and a little careless with emails. Maya's mother: visits one weekend. Nia: Maya's young niece, six years old. The story takes place in an ordinary town over about six weeks of Thursday classes (one Thursday is a holiday with no class, so the story runs about seven weeks), from one Monday to a final Thursday and a little after. Ruth: Maya's older sister, Nia's mother. Mr Bashir: a retired bus driver in the class (he drove the number fourteen route for thirty-one years), sceptical and funny, a widower, who prays five times a day. Lena: a student in the class, anxious about her exams. Mr Lowe: Maya's manager, brisk but fair. Dana: a sharp, fair-minded colleague who asks hard questions. Sam: a new colleague who joins near the end. Fern: Maya's houseplant. Maya's father died five years ago and made terrible pancakes. Maya takes calls from customers at work and has to give a presentation on Wednesday of the fourth week. Maya sits for five minutes each morning with a timer, and later keeps a small smooth pebble from Mrs Adeyemi in her pocket. Key terms: Mindfulness, Autopilot, Anchor, Breath, Body scan, Present moment, Weather, Wave, Pause. Mindfulness practice has roots in Buddhist teaching about two and a half thousand years old, and is taught today in religious and non-religious ways; a hospital programme in the late 1970s helped bring it into modern health care. The science is hedged: studies suggest it helps many people with stress, but not everyone, and it is not a cure. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, calm, concrete and honest; one clear idea in each beat; no claims that anything fixes everything; Mrs Adeyemi never preaches. Beat 200 reminds the reader that this book is general information and not medical advice, and that anyone who feels very low or anxious for a long time should speak to a doctor.

Maya reached three with great satisfaction, and then, without any announcement, her mind slipped away like a cat through a half-open door. She did not notice that it had gone, and so for a while nobody was counting at all.

When she next became aware of herself, she was standing in an imaginary supermarket, frowning at two kinds of pasta and wondering whether she had any tomatoes at home. She had no idea how she had got there, and she had certainly lost count of her breaths. It was almost comic, how completely and how quietly the supermarket had swallowed her.

“I failed completely,” Maya announced at the end of the exercise, “because I only got as far as three.” Mrs Adeyemi, however, asked her a different question, and she asked it very gently, as one might ask a child about a drawing. She wished to know whether Maya had noticed, at some moment, that her thoughts had drifted away.

“Then you did precisely what we are here to do,” said Mrs Adeyemi, and she explained that the moment of noticing is not a failure at all. It is the practice itself, she said, and every time it happens a small muscle of attention grows a little stronger. Maya turned this idea over in her mind and found, to her surprise, that it was a relief.

The mind, Mrs Adeyemi told them, is rather like a young puppy that is forever wandering off to chew a slipper or chase a leaf. There is no point in scolding it, she said, because it does not understand scolding, and the only sensible response is to pick it up and bring it back again and again. Mr Bashir, who had been sitting with his arms folded all evening, smiled for the first time.

What matters, Mrs Adeyemi went on, is not that the mind stays where we put it but that we come back, and that we do so gently. She likened it to a kind teacher who leads a wandering child back to her desk, without anger and without any lecture, as many times as it takes. Harshness, she said, only teaches the child to hide, whereas patience teaches it to return.

Mr Bashir confessed, with a rueful grin, that during the counting his mind had quietly gone off to drive the old number fourteen route that he had driven for thirty-one years. He had stopped at every set of traffic lights and waved at the same newspaper seller, and he had not once reached ten. The circle laughed with him, and it was a warm and friendly sort of laughter.

Lena admitted that her mind was so full of exams that there was hardly any room left for anything else, and her voice wobbled a little. Mrs Adeyemi said honestly that the practice would not take the exams away, but that it might change the way Lena stood among them. “It is the difference,” she said, “between being swept along by a river and learning to stand on the bank.”

On the walk home she found, quite without trying, that she could feel her feet meeting the pavement with every step. She noticed that the left one was sore from a blister she had ignored all day, and she noticed too that the rain had stopped and the street lamps were laying soft orange pools on the wet road. It was a very ordinary evening, and for once, she realised, she was truly inside it.

At home she felt the familiar tug towards her phone, as strong as a magnet's, and she stood in the hallway with her coat half off and her hand halfway to her pocket. Instead of reaching for it, she took one slow, deliberate breath and felt her feet on the old floorboards. It was a very small thing, hardly a victory, but it was the first time she had ever paused there.

On Friday morning she found the card that Mrs Adeyemi had pressed into her hand, propped against the teapot where she could not ignore it. It asked for five minutes a day, in the same place, with a timer, and it ended with the cheerful warning that nobody was expected to be good at it. The idea of being asked to do something so modest and so difficult made her smile.

She sat on the edge of her bed, switched her phone to aeroplane mode so that it could not tempt her, and set the timer for five minutes. Time behaved strangely, stretching and dragging until she was convinced that the timer must be broken, and she opened one eye to check. It had run for ninety seconds, and she had spent most of them rehearsing a conversation with her landlord.

On Saturday she was out from morning until dark, running errands and meeting an old friend, and the card on the table went unread. When she remembered, at ten o'clock at night, her first impulse was to decide that the whole experiment had failed, but she remembered Mrs Adeyemi's puppy. She sat for two minutes instead of five, and two minutes proved a great deal better than none.

On Sunday, the third morning, she carried a mug of tea out to her doorstep and sat in a patch of thin sunlight to practise. About halfway through the five minutes a persistent itch awakened on the side of her nose, small at first and then insistent. Every instinct told her to scratch it, and she felt her hand begin to rise.

Instead of scratching it, she decided to watch it, as carefully as a scientist watches a strange new creature. It tingled, it pulsed, it slid from her nose to her cheek and grew weaker with each breath, until at last it dissolved into nothing at all. She had never once considered that a sensation might change on its own if only she let it.

That afternoon she told her sister Ruth about the itch, and Ruth laughed kindly and said that it sounded like something Nia would find fascinating. A moment later six-year-old Nia had seized the phone and demanded to know whether Auntie had been sitting still like a statue. Maya promised that she had, for almost three minutes, and that statues were a good deal harder than they looked.

On Monday her knees began to ache as she sat cross-legged on the floor, and her first thought was that the whole business was a silly mistake. Instead of leaping up, she noticed the ache, noticed her wish to escape from it and then moved her legs, very slowly and on purpose. It felt like the difference between being pushed around and quietly choosing to step aside.

On Tuesday her mind seemed determined to organise her entire week, producing lists of meetings and bills and a tap that needed mending, one after another, like a juggler with an endless supply of plates. She noticed what it was doing, almost laughed out loud and returned to her breath with something close to affection. It was the fourth time that morning that she had come back, and she had stopped counting it as failure.

On Wednesday evening she glanced at the calendar on her fridge and realised, with a small jolt of surprise, that she was looking forward to Thursday. A week earlier she would have laughed at the idea of choosing to spend an evening sitting in a hall and trying to feel her feet. Something, she thought, had shifted inside her, though she could not have said exactly what it was.

On Thursday evening she walked to the hall, feeling the cool air on her face and the steady rhythm of her own breathing. She arrived ten minutes early, which had never happened to her before in her life, and found Mr Bashir already sitting there polishing his glasses. “I did my five minutes,” he announced, “and I only checked the timer twice.”

Mrs Adeyemi opened the second class by asking how the homework had gone, and the answers came out slowly and honestly. Lena had missed three days, Mr Bashir had missed one, and Maya, who had missed a whole Saturday, confessed it with a sheepish smile. Nobody was scolded, and Mrs Adeyemi merely thanked them for telling the truth, which she said was the first step in any kind of practice.

Mrs Adeyemi had set out a row of mats and soft grey blankets across the floor of the hall, and she explained that tonight they would lie down and travel through the body. It was called a body scan, she said, and it meant moving the attention slowly from one part to the next, as a torch moves across a dark room. Maya lay down with some embarrassment, and felt the cool floor press up against her shoulders.

In a low, even voice Mrs Adeyemi asked them to bring their attention to the toes of the left foot, and then to the sole, the heel and the ankle. She added that they were not trying to relax or to feel anything special, but only to notice whatever happened to be there, even if that was nothing at all. Maya found this oddly freeing, and for a while she simply lay and noticed.

As the attention travelled slowly upwards, Maya discovered that her calves were as hard as rope and that her stomach was clenched like a fist. When she reached her face, she found that her jaw had been locked tight, perhaps for months, and that she had never once noticed. It was like opening a drawer in her own house and finding a room that she had not known was there.

The voice moved on to her hips and her back, and Maya became aware of the sheer weight of her body pressing down into the mat. It occurred to her that the floor was holding her up without any effort and without asking for anything in return, and that she did not have to do the holding herself. She let out a long breath, and some small hard thing inside her shifted.

Somewhere around her shoulders the voice grew faint and distant, and Maya slipped into a deep and dreamless sleep. The small brass bell dragged her back to the hall, and for a moment she did not know where she was or why she was lying on a floor. Then she heard a soft, rhythmic snore and realised, with a rush of embarrassment, that it was her own.

Maya apologised in a whisper, but Mrs Adeyemi only smiled and said that tiredness was part of the practice too. It was information, she said, and perhaps Maya's body had been asking for more sleep than she had been willing to give it. She suggested that next time Maya might try the exercise sitting up, and that she should also be a little kinder to her evenings.

After a short break for tea, Mrs Adeyemi asked them to sit and listen, simply listen, to whatever sounds reached the hall. She asked them not to name the sounds or to decide whether they liked them, but to let each one arrive and pass, like waves reaching a beach. For some reason this seemed far harder than lying on the floor and feeling their feet.

Maya heard rain trickling down a pipe outside, the creak of a chair under someone's shifting weight and the faint rumble of a train far across the town. Her mind rushed to attach a story to each of them, so that the train became a journey and the creak became somebody's boredom, but she gently set the stories aside. What remained was simply sound, rising and falling, with no one telling her what it meant.

Afterwards Lena said that she had always thought of silence as an empty space, whereas tonight it had seemed full to the brim with small sounds. Mr Bashir added solemnly that the loudest sound he had heard was his own stomach grumbling about its supper, and the whole circle burst into helpless laughter. It was, Maya thought as she gathered her coat, the happiest silence she had ever been part of.

On Friday morning Maya settled into her seat on the bus, zipped her phone deep into her bag and, feeling faintly absurd, raised her eyes. She had no plan beyond paying attention, and she half expected to be bored within a minute. Instead she found that the bus was full of things that she had been travelling past for years.

She heard the low hum of the engine, the hydraulic sigh of the doors and, somewhere behind her, the bright laughter of a small child. A thin thread of music leaked from a stranger's headphones, and beneath everything ran the steady murmur of a dozen quiet conversations. Never before had the bus sounded to her like a place where real people lived.

She watched two raindrops race each other down the window, one hesitating and the other plunging, until they merged and ran on together. Across the aisle a man in a green scarf was reading a battered paperback, and he smiled quietly at something on the page. The whole scene was so small and so ordinary that she wondered how she had missed it a thousand times.

At the next stop the woman with the pushchair, the same woman who had smiled at her on that rushed Monday, climbed aboard and wedged herself into the space beside Maya. This time Maya looked up in time to meet her eyes, and the two of them exchanged a small, genuine smile while the baby waved a woollen mitten. It was a tiny moment, and yet it felt like a door that had been standing open for weeks.

At lunchtime she carried a bowl of lentil soup out to a bench beside the office instead of eating at her desk. She lifted the first spoonful slowly and let herself notice its heat, its salt, the faint bite of pepper and the soft grain of the lentils against her tongue. It was a meal she had probably eaten a hundred times and had never once tasted.

Halfway through the bowl her hand crept towards her phone, as it always did when she was alone, and she watched it go with a kind of amused interest. She set the phone face down on the bench and returned to the soup, which had cooled slightly and was no less good for that. When the bowl was empty she felt satisfied in a way that a hurried sandwich had never made her feel.

On Monday morning, in the middle of a difficult report, Maya suddenly noticed that her shoulders had crept almost up to her ears and that her jaw was clenched so hard that her teeth ached. She had been sitting like that for what felt like an hour, and she had no idea when it had begun. It was as though her body had been shouting for some time, and she had only now turned her head to listen.

She let her shoulders fall and her jaw loosen, and then she drew one slow breath all the way down into her stomach. The dull headache behind her eyes did not vanish, but it seemed to lose some of its grip, as a hand relaxes when it is no longer being squeezed. She wondered how many headaches she had endured simply because she had not noticed their cause.

Maya began to understand that stress very often announces itself in the body long before the mind is willing to admit it. Her shoulders and her jaw became a kind of early warning bell, ringing quietly whenever the pressure began to rise. If she could only learn to hear it sooner, she thought, she might have time to do something kind about it.

Mr Lowe stopped by her desk, set down a thick folder and asked whether she would present the quarter's results to the whole office on Wednesday of the following week. She said yes at once, because she always said yes, but her hands turned cold and her stomach gave a small and unmistakable flutter. For the first time she noticed how quickly her body knew what was coming, and how quietly it had warned her.

On Tuesday afternoon an email from Joe arrived with the wrong date in it again, and this time he had copied in the entire team. The tone was brisk and careless, as though the mistake were somebody else's, and Maya felt the old heat climbing up her neck. She could already see herself answering, and she could already see what the answer would say.

Her fingers began to fly across the keyboard, and the words appeared on the screen almost without her permission, hot and sharp and perfectly deserved. “Joe, this is the fourth time, and I am tired of cleaning up after you,” the message said, and her finger hovered over the button. Something, a faint memory of a hall full of quiet, made her stop just in time.

She noticed that her face was hot, her heart was beating faster than usual and her shoulders had crept up again towards her ears. She pressed her feet into the floor, as she had learned to do in the hall, and took one slow breath all the way down. That small gap, hardly longer than a heartbeat, was what Mrs Adeyemi called a pause, and it felt like stepping out of a rushing river onto a stone.

She deleted the angry message, one furious word at a time, and sat for a moment with the empty box in front of her. Then she wrote a short and perfectly polite reply that gave the correct date, thanked Joe for his work and asked whether they might check the next one together before it went out. She read it through once and sent it, and her shoulders sank a full inch.

Within minutes Joe had replied, and his message was nothing like the one she had braced herself for. He apologised plainly, admitted that he had been rushing through everything for weeks and promised to check his dates before he sent anything else. Maya read it twice and realised that the angry message would have started a war, whereas the calm one had ended an argument before it began.

On the bus home she thought about what had happened, and she saw that the pause had not removed her annoyance at all. The annoyance had been quite real and had sat in her chest for a while, but the pause had given her a little room in which to choose her response. Between what happens and what we do, she discovered, there is a space, and the space is where freedom begins.

At the third class Mrs Adeyemi drew a sun, a cloud and a streak of rain on the whiteboard and compared our feelings to the weather. A storm of anger, she said, or a cloud of worry, will arrive, change and pass, but the sky that holds them remains wide and untouched. We are tempted to believe that we are the weather, when really we are closer to the sky.

Mr Bashir, who had said very little about himself until that evening, remarked quietly that the sky in his own life had been foggy for some time, ever since his wife had died. Mrs Adeyemi thanked him with great simplicity and said that the sky is never harmed by the fog, however thick the fog may feel, and that even the heaviest weather is not the whole of the day. The circle was silent, and it was a respectful and tender kind of silence.

Mrs Adeyemi invited each of them to name the weather inside them at that moment, and the answers came round the circle one by one. Lena said “stormy but clearing,” Mr Bashir said “misty,” and Maya, after a long and honest moment, said “grey and windy, with a few sunny spells.” It was strange how much lighter it felt to describe her feelings as weather than to be inside them.

Lena said that it comforted her to think that her worry was only passing weather and that it would not last for ever. Mrs Adeyemi agreed warmly, but she added a careful word, which was that some weather is very heavy and very long, and that nobody should try to carry it alone. Talking to a friend, a doctor or a counsellor, she said, is not a failure of the practice but a sensible use of it.

After the third class Maya stayed behind to help stack the chairs, and while they worked she told Mrs Adeyemi about the presentation that was waiting for her the following Wednesday. She tried to sound casual, but her voice wobbled on the word “whole,” as in the whole office. Mrs Adeyemi set down her chair carefully and gave her undivided and unhurried attention.

Mrs Adeyemi asked where Maya felt the worry, and Maya said that it lived in her stomach and fluttered there like a trapped moth. Her teacher suggested that she should simply name it, quietly and without argument, by saying to herself that worry was here. Naming a feeling, she explained, creates a small space between the feeling and the person who feels it.

Maya admitted that she had always thought acceptance meant giving up, and she asked Mrs Adeyemi whether she was supposed to simply put up with everything. Mrs Adeyemi shook her head and explained that acceptance only means seeing clearly what is true at this moment, whether you like it or not. From that honest place, she said, you can decide calmly what to do next.

Mrs Adeyemi smiled and offered an image that Maya would remember for a long time. A ship's captain, she said, cannot possibly choose a course until he knows exactly where the ship is, and pretending to be somewhere else only leads to the rocks. Acceptance is simply the act of looking at the map and finding the small red dot that says you are here.

Maya confessed that a thought kept repeating itself in her head, which was that she would freeze in front of everyone and forget every word. Mrs Adeyemi pointed out that this was a thought and not a prediction, and certainly not a fact, because the mind produces thousands of thoughts a day and believes only a few of them. She suggested trying the phrase, “I am having the thought that I will freeze.”

At home on Friday evening she tried the sentence aloud in her kitchen, feeling slightly ridiculous. “I am having the thought that I will freeze,” she said, and the words changed the thought from a fact into something that was merely passing through her head, like a bus passing a window. The thought did not leave her altogether, but she could feel that it had loosened its hold on her, and that was enough for one evening.

On Saturday she stood in the living room and delivered the entire presentation to her houseplant, Fern, who proved an attentive if unresponsive audience. She kept her feet planted on the floor and her breath low and steady while she spoke, and her words came out slower and clearer than they had in her head. By the third run-through she was almost, to her own astonishment, enjoying herself a little.

On Sunday she walked in the park, where the sunlight lay in long gold bars across the grass, and the worry rushed back as strong as ever. She sat down on a bench, reminded herself that it was weather and nothing more, and let it blow through her without arguing and without trying to push it away. After ten minutes it had thinned a little, and a blackbird was singing in the hedge.

By Tuesday night the slides were finished, the notes were printed and her bag was packed by the front door. She could not sleep, so she lay in the dark with one hand on her stomach, following the slow rise and fall of her breath. She did not decide that she would sleep, because that would only have woken her, and sometime after midnight she did.

On Wednesday morning she woke with the flutter already beating in her stomach, as if it had been waiting for her all night. “Worry is here,” she said quietly, and she put two slices of bread into the toaster and stood watching them, and nothing else, until they turned golden. She buttered the toast, and she tasted it, and it was the best breakfast she had eaten in a very long time.

On the way to work she felt her feet meet the pavement and the cool morning air brush her face. The flutter was still beating in her stomach, but she let it travel beside her like an anxious friend, neither pushing it away nor handing it the steering wheel. It was, she thought, a slightly different way of being frightened, and a rather more bearable one.

At two o'clock the meeting room filled with colleagues, scraping chairs and murmuring and settling their coffee cups on the long table. Mr Lowe took a seat at the back with his arms folded, Joe gave her an encouraging nod and sharp-eyed Dana opened her notebook and uncapped a pen. Maya's mouth was suddenly as dry as paper, and her notes seemed to shiver in her hand.

Before she opened her mouth, Maya stood quite still at the front of the room and pressed her feet down into the carpet. She took one slow breath, all the way to the bottom of her stomach, and in that single moment of stillness the room seemed to hold its own breath for her. It was the same quiet that she had met in the hall on Thursday evenings, and it had followed her here.

She began, and her voice shook a little, which she noticed at once and which, a month earlier, would have sent her spiralling into panic. Instead she told herself calmly that the shaking was weather, that it would pass, and that it did not need to be fixed before she could speak. She kept going, and slowly, sentence by sentence, the tremor settled into a steady voice.

Halfway through, she lost her place completely, and for a long and terrible second the room was silent and every face turned expectantly towards her. She did not rush and she did not apologise, but simply took a breath and felt her feet, and the next sentence floated back to her like a leaf returning to the surface of a pond. Nobody seemed to have noticed the gap, or if they had, nobody seemed to mind it at all.

Dana, who never accepted an easy answer, leant forward and asked a sharp question about one of the figures, and Maya felt a surge of old fear. Instead of rushing to speak, she paused for a single breath, and then she said honestly what she knew and what she would need to look up. Dana nodded slowly, apparently satisfied, and wrote something down in her notebook with a small, approving mark.

When she finished, the room broke into applause, and Joe grinned from the second row and raised his thumb. Maya's hands were still trembling, and her heart was still hammering, but she let them tremble and hammer and did not try to hide either. They would settle in their own time, she thought, just as weather does, and there was no need to hurry them.

Afterwards Mr Lowe stopped her in the corridor and told her, in his brisk way, that her presentation had been clear and steady. Maya thanked him and said nothing about the flutter, which had never really left her, but which for once had not been allowed to take the controls. It was not the absence of fear that had carried her through, she realised, but the company of it.

At the fourth class Maya told the circle about her presentation, and Lena, who had been listening with shining eyes, cheered out loud. Mr Bashir folded his arms and said, with the teasing grin that she had come to like, “So it fixed you, then.” Everyone looked at Mrs Adeyemi, who laughed warmly and shook her head, as if she had been waiting for exactly that question.

“No,” she said, “and I would be doing you a disservice if I let you think so.” Mindfulness does not remove problems, she told them, and the research on it is mixed, because many studies suggest that it helps with stress and low mood, whereas others find little benefit. What it offers is a different relationship with difficulty, and that, she added, is a more modest promise and a more honest one.

Before they left, Mrs Adeyemi added a careful warning that she said she would not leave out. Sitting quietly can sometimes stir up painful memories and strong feelings, she explained, and anyone who finds this too much should go gently, stop if they need to and talk to a doctor or a counsellor. The practice is a tool, she repeated, and not a cure, and there is no shame in asking for more.

On Friday evening the queue at the supermarket stretched almost to the bread aisle, and a chorus of sighs and shuffling rose from the people waiting. In the old days Maya would have pulled out her phone within seconds and scrolled through nothing at all, but tonight she let it lie in her pocket. She had a curious feeling that she was about to be given a free five minutes.

She felt her feet on the hard floor and followed three slow breaths while the queue shuffled forward a step at a time. When she looked up, she noticed for the first time that the young cashier had dark circles under her eyes and a plaster on one finger, and that she had probably been standing there for hours. A small, unexpected wave of kindness rose in her, and she decided that she would smile when her turn came.

The queue moved no faster than before, and yet the waiting felt shorter, and almost welcome, as though it had been turned from an obstacle into a small private practice. When she finally reached the till, she thanked the cashier warmly and asked how her day had been, and the young woman looked up with startled pleasure. It cost her nothing at all, and yet it changed the temperature of the whole exchange.

That evening her phone buzzed on the kitchen table while she was stirring a pan of pasta, and she felt an immediate and powerful urge to pick it up. Her hand had actually begun to move before her mind had caught up, and her heart was beating with a small, greedy excitement. It might have been anything, which was exactly what made it so hard to ignore.

Instead of obeying the urge, she stood still with the wooden spoon in her hand and watched it, as a surfer might watch a wave approaching. It rose, it swelled to a peak that felt almost unbearable, it wobbled and then it fell away, and the whole thing was over in about a minute. She had always assumed that such urges grew until they were satisfied, and she had been wrong.

She carried the phone into the bedroom, shut the door on it and sat down to eat her pasta at the table with nothing to look at but the food. When she checked it afterwards, she found that the message had been a promotional offer for a pair of shoes, and that the urgent thing had been nothing at all. She laughed aloud in the empty kitchen, and the sound of her own laughter was surprisingly good to hear.

On Saturday Maya waited on the platform for her mother's train, and for once she did not reach for her phone to fill the empty minutes. She noticed the pigeons strutting along the rails, the crackle of the announcements and the warm smell of coffee drifting from the kiosk. When the train drew in and her mother stepped down with a suitcase, Maya was already looking in exactly the right direction.

Over tea her mother talked about her garden, her neighbour's cat, which had taken to sleeping in the greenhouse, and a new variety of runner bean that had done surprisingly well. Maya listened without composing her reply, without glancing at the clock and without waiting for a gap in which to talk about herself. She simply heard her mother's voice, which she realised she had not really heard for years.

In the middle of a sentence about the beans, Maya's mother stopped and studied her daughter's face with her head tilted to one side. “You are listening,” she said slowly, as though it were a fascinating discovery, “really listening, aren't you?” Maya felt tears prick behind her eyes, and she nodded, because it was true, and because it was such a small thing to have been missing for so long.

Maya explained about the Thursday class to her mother, who raised one doubtful eyebrow and asked whether it was anything like those relaxation tapes. “It sounds very odd to me,” she admitted, “but I will say that you look calmer than you did at Christmas.” Coming from a woman who gave compliments as rarely as she gave away her recipes, it was high praise.

That evening they cooked together in Maya's small kitchen, bumping elbows and laughing, and her mother told a story that Maya had not heard for years. It concerned Maya's father, who had made the worst pancakes in the history of cooking, flat and grey and leathery, and who had served them every Sunday with enormous pride. They were both laughing so hard that the onions were completely forgotten on the board.

On Sunday they strolled through the market among the pyramids of apples and the buckets of flowers, and Maya heard Mrs Adeyemi's voice in her memory. Full attention, she had said, is one of the greatest gifts that we can give to another person, and it costs nothing but our willingness to put down our own plans. Maya found that she wanted to give it, and that it was easier than she had expected.

On a bench at the edge of the market her mother said quietly that she had been very lonely after the funeral, lonelier than she had ever let anyone know. Maya listened without interrupting once, without hurrying to console and without composing the clever sentence that would make everything better. She understood, with a clarity that surprised her, that her mother did not need a solution but a witness.

Maya did not try to fix anything and did not offer a single piece of advice, for she could feel that advice would have been a way of escaping the moment. She said only that it sounded very hard, and her mother squeezed her hand and smiled through the tears that had gathered in her eyes. They sat on in a silence that was full rather than empty, while the market carried on around them.

On Sunday evening Maya hugged her mother goodbye on the platform and stood waving until the train had dwindled into the dusk. A lump rose in her throat, hard and warm, and instead of swallowing it down she let it sit there and breathed around it. She walked home slowly, tired and tender, and that night she was too worn out to sit, and so she let the practice slide for the first time.

On Monday morning Maya answered a call at the front desk, and a customer began shouting about a delay in his order before she had even finished saying hello. The delay was not her fault, and he was not interested in whose fault it was, and each loud sentence landed on her like a handful of gravel. She felt a hot, familiar anger rising to meet him, as fast and as fierce as it ever had.

Even while the man was still shouting, Maya noticed what was happening in her body. Her face was hot, her chest was tight, her hands had curled into fists beneath the desk and her heart was racing like a drum. It struck her that the anger had begun in her body a full second before it reached her words, and that this second was a gift.

She took one slow breath and pressed her feet to the floor, and in the gap that this opened up she asked herself what she actually wished to say. She did not wish to shout back, which would have felt satisfying for about four seconds, and she did not wish to grovel either. She chose her words as carefully as a person chooses stepping stones across a stream.

She told him calmly that she was sorry about the delay and that she would do everything in her power to sort it out that day. The man grumbled and drew breath, and although he did not thank her, his voice grew quieter, and the call ended without another raised word. Afterwards her hands trembled a little, and she let them tremble, and Joe appeared silently at her elbow with a biscuit.

On Tuesday Maya walked to the station to catch a train to a meeting in another town, and instead of rushing, she let her attention rest on the small facts of the journey. She noticed her feet on the pavement, the sharpness of the cool air in her nose and the low light sliding across the wet stones. It occurred to her that this ordinary street had been here all the time, patiently waiting to be seen.

Steam was pouring from a grating outside the bakery, curling and dissolving in the cold air, and the smell of warm bread drifted across the street like an invitation. Beyond it, low sunlight lay on a brick wall like honey spread on toast, turning the whole corner into something faintly golden. She felt a small, quiet joy, and she knew that it had been available to her on every morning of her life.

A robin was perched on an iron railing, studying her with its head on one side, and at her feet a puddle held a perfect, trembling patch of blue sky. She stopped to look, and an elderly man behind her tutted and stepped around her, which made her smile rather than apologise. These small things were not hidden, she thought, and nobody had taken them away, but she had been far too busy to look.

On Wednesday evening she glanced at the little card propped against the teapot and realised that four whole days had passed since she had last sat down to practise. Her mother's visit, the shouting customer and a heap of tiredness had pushed it from her mind, and the days had slid by one after another like beads on a thread. A familiar voice inside her began, almost at once, to speak in a tone of cold and weary disappointment.

A wave of guilt washed over her, and the harsh voice in her head declared that she had ruined everything, that she was no good at this and that she should never have started. It was the same voice that had once told her she would freeze in front of the whole office, and it was no more truthful now than it had been then. Even so, it took her some time to remember that she did not have to believe it.

At the fifth class Maya confessed, with her eyes lowered, that she had missed four whole days of practice, and she waited for the gentle disappointment she expected to see. Mrs Adeyemi, however, only nodded and said, quite simply, that there was nothing to do except begin again. She spoke as though she were giving directions to a nearby street rather than passing judgment.

Mrs Adeyemi explained that every moment in which we notice that we have drifted is itself a beginning, and that no one ever has to go back to the start of the road. You do not return to zero, she said, because everything that you have already learned goes with you, as surely as the ability to ride a bicycle survives a long winter. The only thing that is lost by missing four days is the guilt we add on top.

Mrs Adeyemi asked Maya how she would speak to a friend who had missed four days of something she cared about, and the question was so simple that Maya answered before she could think. She would tell her friend not to worry, she said, that it did not matter in the least, and that she could start again whenever she wished. Mrs Adeyemi waited a moment in silence, and Maya heard for herself the gap between how she treated a friend and how she treated herself.

Mrs Adeyemi invited them to place one hand on the centre of the chest, to feel its warmth and to say silently some words of kindness to themselves. Maya chose the phrase “may I be gentle with myself,” which she would have found embarrassing a month earlier, and felt her throat tighten and then slowly relax. It was strange to receive, from her own voice, the tone that she had so often reserved for others.

Mr Bashir announced gruffly that the exercise was silly and that he had felt like a fool saying such things to himself in a room full of strangers. After a moment, however, he admitted with a reluctant half-smile that he had also felt something warm in his chest, as though a heater had been switched on. The circle laughed softly with him, and Maya felt a rush of gratitude for his honesty and his stubbornness.

Lena asked whether she needed a special cushion, or a candle, or perhaps a perfectly quiet room in which to practise properly. Mrs Adeyemi smiled and said that there was no special place, and that a kitchen chair, a bus seat or a bench in the park would serve just as well. The only essential equipment, she told them, was a willingness to stop for a moment.

A few minutes every day, Mrs Adeyemi said, would do more for them than one long session once in a blue moon. A plant does better with a little water each day than with a flood once a month, and attention is a habit that grows by repetition and not by heroic effort. Maya, who had planned to make up for her four missed days with a single hour, put down her pen and thought about that.

Mr Bashir asked, with his usual directness, where all of this really came from, and Mrs Adeyemi answered him with equal directness. Mindfulness, she said, has its roots in Buddhist teaching that is about two and a half thousand years old, where it has been practised and refined by monks, nuns and ordinary people across many countries. She wanted them to know that she was borrowing from a great tradition and not inventing something of her own.

She added, with care, that many other traditions also prize the training of attention in their own ways, and that she would not claim any of them as a rival or a copy. Prayer, contemplation and quiet reflection are found in faiths all over the world, she said, and each tradition understands its practice in its own terms. Nobody in this hall was being asked to accept anyone else's explanation of what was happening inside them.

Mr Bashir, to the surprise of nobody who knew him well, said that he prayed five times a day and that those moments were the steadiest attention he had ever given to anything. He was quite happy, he said, to borrow this new tool for his wandering mind, so long as nobody asked him to give up his faith. Mrs Adeyemi bowed her head to him, and said that she would never dream of asking.

Mrs Adeyemi explained that modern courses of this kind, taught without any religious language, grew out of a hospital programme in the late 1970s that was designed for people with long-term pain and stress. You could take the practice as a plain skill, she said, or you could place it inside your own faith, and both ways were perfectly honourable. She finished by reminding them that the following Thursday was a holiday, and that they would meet again in two weeks.

On Friday at work she slipped away to the stairwell, a bare concrete corridor where nobody ever went, and sat down on a middle step to practise for three minutes. There was no cushion, no incense and no bell, only a cold rail, the echo of a distant door and her own slow breathing. It counted, she decided, just as much as any hour in a quiet and candlelit hall.

That night she woke at three in the morning with her mind already running like a hamster on a wheel, spinning through money, work and every thing that might possibly go wrong in the coming year. The harder she tried to command her thoughts to stop, the faster they ran, and the more tired and desperate she became. It was exactly the kind of battle that nobody ever wins, however stubborn they are.

Instead of fighting the sleeplessness, she turned her attention to her body, to the weight of her arms and legs, the warmth of the blanket and the slow movement of her breath. She made no promise to herself that she would fall asleep, because she understood that promises of that kind are only another way of pushing. She simply lay there in the dark and rested, whether sleep came to her or not.

Towards dawn she may have dozed, though she could never afterwards be certain, and when the alarm went off she felt tired but not defeated. Resting quietly had not given her a full night's sleep, and she did not pretend that it had, but it had saved her from the exhaustion of a night spent in combat. The day that followed felt gentler than it would otherwise have been, and she was grateful for that.

On Monday, while the kettle boiled in the office kitchen, Joe leant against the counter and told her that she seemed different somehow, calmer and a good deal less hunted. He asked her, quite sincerely and without any trace of mockery, what had changed. Maya stopped stirring her tea, because it was an honest question, and she wanted to give an honest answer.

She explained, in the simplest words that she could find, about the Thursday class, the breathing and the slow practice of noticing where her mind had gone. She told him plainly that it was not a miracle and not a cure, but that it had helped her to stop living quite so much on autopilot. Joe listened with his head tilted, sceptical but interested, and asked for the name of the hall.

Maya decided to try doing one thing at a time, which she had always dismissed as a luxury for people with less to do. She wrote one email until it was finished, made one phone call with her whole attention and ate her lunch afterwards without a screen in sight. The rhythm was strangely peaceful, like moving from one stepping stone to the next instead of leaping across a river.

At first it felt slower, as though she were walking when everyone else was running, and yet by the end of the day she had finished more than she usually did. Her head buzzed less and she made fewer mistakes, though she was honest enough to admit that one good day proved very little. Still, it was a promising experiment, and she decided to repeat it the next morning and the next.

Joe, who had never been seen to close a window in his life, tried the idea for himself and shut down twelve open tabs, one after another, with the air of a man tidying an attic. He finished his report by three o'clock, a full two hours ahead of schedule, and looked as astonished as if he had found money in an old coat. “Don't tell anyone,” he whispered, “but I think it works, and I think I might be a convert.”

At the coffee machine Dana, who noticed everything and mentioned perhaps a third of it, remarked that Maya had stopped sighing every five minutes. Maya had never realised that she sighed at all, and she laughed with a mixture of embarrassment and delight. It was a strange thing to be told that she had changed by a person who had never once tried to flatter her.

On Tuesday morning, in the middle of an unusually busy hour, Maya reached for a file and caught her cup with her elbow. The hot coffee ran across the desk in a brown tide, dripped over the edge onto the floor and flooded down the front of her clean white shirt. For a split second the old Maya rose in her throat, ready to curse and slam and ruin the morning.

But there was a pause, as there now so often was, and in that pause Maya looked down at the brown wreckage of her shirt and, to her own astonishment, began to laugh. Joe laughed too, helplessly, and the two of them mopped up the desk with a pile of tissues while Dana watched them from across the room with one eyebrow raised. It was the best laugh that Maya had had in the office all year.

She remembered the grey cardigan that lived in her bottom drawer for cold days, buttoned it over the stained shirt and carried on with her work as though nothing at all had happened. By lunchtime the incident had shrunk to a funny story that she told to anyone who would listen. She realised that the coffee had been a matter of a few minutes, and that only the cursing would have made it a matter of a whole ruined day.

On Wednesday evening Maya's phone lit up with a message from Lena, who had sat the first of her exams that morning. She had taken three slow breaths before turning over the paper, she wrote, and for once she had felt as if she were standing on the bank of the river instead of being swept along by it. She did not know how she had done, but she knew that she had been there.

On the holiday Thursday Maya woke slowly, in a bar of pale light from the curtains, and glanced at the date on her phone. She remembered at once that it was five years to the day since her father had died, and the knowledge settled on her chest like a stone. The old habit of busyness rose up to meet it, ready to bury the whole day in errands.

The sadness arrived like a heavy wet coat, and it hung on her shoulders and would not be shaken off. The old Maya would have rushed to fill the day with chores and calls and television, with anything that might drown the feeling in noise. She stood in the middle of her kitchen and, with great difficulty and some fear, decided to do something different.

She sat down on the sofa, wrapped herself in a blanket and let the sadness be there, without trying to explain it or argue with it or rush it on its way. She noticed where it lived, in a heaviness behind her breastbone and a tightness in her throat, and she breathed around those places and let the tears come. It was weather, she told herself, and this was simply a day for rain, and rain has never harmed the sky.

The sadness did not disappear, and she had not expected it to, but it changed and shifted as the morning went on, like clouds rearranging themselves across a wide sky. She made a mug of tea, sat by the window with her hands wrapped around it and heard the birds begin to sing in the plane tree outside. Both things were true together, the grief and the birdsong, and neither cancelled the other.

Around noon she had an unexpected idea, which was to make pancakes in her father's honour, using no recipe and a great deal of optimism. They came out of the pan flat and grey and leathery, precisely as his had always done, and she stood over them with a spatula, laughing and crying at the same time. It was, she decided, a perfect failure, and a very loving one, and she would not have changed a single crumb.

She sat down at the table, poured a lake of syrup over the dreadful pancake and ate it slowly, tasting every leathery mouthful. She laughed and cried at once, and she did not try to decide which one was the real feeling, because she saw that both were true and both were welcome. It was, she thought, the closest she had felt to her father in a very long time.

In the middle of the afternoon she remembered something Mrs Adeyemi had said in the hall, that the practice was a tool and never a replacement for other kinds of support. She did not want to sit alone with her grief all evening, and she understood that reaching for another person was not a failure of her practice but one of its wisest moves. She picked up her phone, found her sister's name and pressed the green button before she could change her mind.

The two sisters talked for forty minutes, about their father's terrible pancakes, his off-key singing in the car and the way he had always carried a spare umbrella for strangers. Ruth admitted that she had cried in her own car that morning in the car park, and that she had been wondering whether to ring, and was very glad that Maya had called first. Neither of them said anything clever or wise, and neither of them needed to, because being heard was enough.

Maya understood that today's sadness was the natural sadness of a day that mattered, and that it was not the same as a heaviness that sets in for weeks and will not lift. If that ever happened to her, she told herself firmly, she would go to see her doctor, and she would feel no more shame about it than about a broken wrist. Knowing when to ask for help, she thought, was every bit as much a part of the skill as knowing how to sit still.

Before the call ended, the sisters planned a picnic with Nia in the park on Saturday, a small celebration of their father and of being alive on a good day. On Friday night Maya packed a wicker basket with sandwiches, apples, a flask of hot chocolate and a bag of slightly burnt, deeply sentimental pancakes. She went to bed that night feeling that something very heavy had been put gently down.

On Saturday in the park, just as Maya spread the blanket on the grass, the first fat drops of rain splashed across it, and within a minute the heavens had opened. There was no question of a picnic in such a downpour, and Maya, Ruth and little Nia stood in a huddle, holding the basket over their heads like a roof. The day that they had been looking forward to all week was gone in ninety seconds.

Maya felt disappointment sink through her stomach like a stone in a pond, heavy and sour and slightly childish. She named it silently, since she knew by now that naming gave it less power over her, and then she saw that Nia's lower lip had begun to tremble. It was a good moment, she thought, to remember that she was not the only person in the park.

Then, with a deliberate breath, Maya looked at the day that she actually had instead of the one that she had planned. The air smelt of wet earth and cut grass, Nia had discovered a puddle and was stamping in it with an expression of pure joy, and Ruth, laughing helplessly under a sagging umbrella, looked ten years younger. Nothing was wrong with this day, she realised, except that it was different from the day she had expected.

The three of them ran to Ruth's flat, dripping and shrieking with laughter, and spread the blanket across the middle of the kitchen floor. They ate sandwiches and apples and drank hot chocolate from the flask while the rain drummed on the window, and Nia declared it by far the best picnic of her whole life. Even Maya's leathery pancakes, which Nia pronounced “interesting,” found a fond and appreciative audience.

On the last Thursday evening the class gathered in the hall for the sixth and final time, and the circle of chairs looked more like a gathering of old friends than a group of strangers. Mr Bashir arrived with a large tin of homemade biscuits, which he presented with solemn dignity and without any explanation. Everyone understood that it was his way of saying something that he could not easily say in words.

Mrs Adeyemi asked each of them to name one small thing that had changed during the six weeks, and the answers came gently round the circle. Lena spoke of the three slow breaths she took before every exam paper, Mr Bashir of his minute of stillness beside the kettle every morning, and Maya of the pause that had saved her from a hundred sharp words. They were all small things, and they were all, she thought, in their own quiet way, quite enormous.

Mrs Adeyemi told them that the course was ending, but that the practice would go with them wherever they went, and that nobody would be issued a certificate for it. Instead she passed round a small basket of smooth grey pebbles and invited each of them to choose one and keep it in a pocket as a reminder to come back. Maya's fingers closed around hers, which was warm from the hand of the person before.

For the last time they sat together in silence, for twenty minutes, which would have seemed impossible to Maya only six weeks before. Her mind wandered many times, to the supermarket and her father and a pile of laundry, and many times she brought it back with the gentleness of a teacher leading a child to her desk. She no longer counted either the wandering or the returning, for she had learned that both were simply the practice.

Before they left, Mrs Adeyemi told them honestly that there would be days, perhaps weeks, when they forgot everything that they had learned and drifted back into autopilot. This was entirely normal, she said, and the remedy was always the same, which was to notice, to breathe and to begin again. She also reminded them that if life ever felt too heavy, they should talk to a doctor or someone they trusted.

At the goodbyes Mr Bashir shook Maya's hand firmly and said, with great dignity, that it was not magic but that he was glad he had come. Lena swapped telephone numbers with both of them and promised that they would meet for tea next month, and then Maya stepped out into the cool dark street. She walked home under the lamps with her fingers closed around the pebble, feeling every step.

On the Monday after the last class the alarm rang at exactly the same hour as it had on that first rushed Monday, in the same small bedroom with the same crooked curtains. The pebble sat on her bedside table, cool and smooth, and for the first time in years she picked it up before she reached for her phone. She held it in her palm for a long moment, and she felt her feet against the sheet.

In the kitchen she made toast again, exactly as she had done on that first Monday, except that her phone lay face down on the far side of the counter. She stood beside the toaster and watched the bread turn golden, buttered it slowly while the butter melted into small bright pools, and then tasted every mouthful. It was the same toast and the same kitchen, and it was a different morning entirely.

Maya left the flat with ten minutes to spare, which was an arrangement she had once believed to be impossible, and walked unhurriedly to the bus stop. She stood in the thin morning sunshine with her hands in her pockets and waited, with nothing to do and nothing to check and, to her surprise, nothing to dread. When the bus came round the corner at last, it looked to her like an old and rather dependable friend.

At work nothing had changed at all, not one thing that anyone could have pointed to. The same emails were waiting in the same untidy queue, Joe was still delightfully careless with his dates and Mr Lowe still strode past her desk with a folder under his arm. What had changed was Maya, who was now actually present for her own morning, and who found that a familiar and demanding world looked quite different from the inside.

On Wednesday Mr Lowe added a sudden deadline to an already overloaded day, and Maya found herself sliding back into the old habits. She skipped her walk, swallowed her lunch at her desk in four minutes and felt her shoulders climb steadily towards her ears. She would have liked to say that her practice had made her immune, but the day had not read the instructions.

When Joe asked her a small and perfectly reasonable question, Maya answered with one sharp sentence that was out of her mouth before she could catch it. This time, however, she noticed almost in the same breath, took one slow breath, felt her feet and turned to Joe with a rueful apology before the sharpness could settle. He waved a hand and said that there was nothing to apologise for, and they both laughed, and the afternoon carried on lighter than it had begun.

That evening Maya understood that there would always be rushing days, tangled mornings and sharp afternoons, and that she would never be finished with them. The difference now was that she noticed sooner and that she knew the road home, which led through a breath, a pair of feet and a gentle beginning again. She no longer needed to be perfect, and that was the greatest relief of all.

A new colleague called Sam arrived that week, and by the middle of his first morning he looked as flustered as a man who has been dropped into a river. Maya did not deliver a lecture about breathing or attention, since she had learned that nobody wants to be taught in the middle of a flood. She offered him a cup of tea, showed him where the kettle lived and told him that the first week is always the hardest.

On Saturday Maya met Lena and Mr Bashir at a small café in the park, and the three of them sat with their mugs and compared notes on the weeks since the final class. Lena had passed two of her three exams and was calm about the third, and Mr Bashir announced that he now drove the old number fourteen route in his head only when he chose to. It was a real pleasure, Maya thought, to be among people who understood without being told.

Walking home through the park in the late afternoon, Maya realised with a small start that she had not looked at her phone for twenty minutes, and that it had cost her no effort whatever. Her hand was resting on the pebble in her coat pocket, as naturally as another person's might have rested on a rail, and the light was falling in long gold bars across the grass. She breathed in slowly and deeply, and for that moment she was exactly where she was.

On Sunday evening Ruth brought Nia to stay the night, kissed them both and hurried away to catch an early shift. Tomorrow was Nia's first day in a new class at a new school, and she stood in the hallway clutching her toy rabbit, unusually quiet and a little pale. Maya recognised the look at once, since she had worn it herself for most of her adult life.

In the spare bed Nia could not settle, because her small mind kept racing ahead to tomorrow and showing her a dozen frightening pictures. What if nobody talked to her, she whispered, and what if she got lost on the way to the toilet, and what if the teacher was cross? Maya sat on the edge of the bed, and felt a rush of love and a flicker of recognition.

Maya asked whether Nia would like to learn something silly and clever that grown-ups sometimes forget. She laid a small warm hand on Nia's tummy and explained that it would swell like a balloon when she breathed in and shrink again when she breathed out. Nia giggled and began to practise, solemnly, with her tongue between her teeth, and together they counted three slow breaths, in and out.

Maya asked Nia to wiggle her toes and to feel the blanket pressing against them, and Nia obeyed with a look of intense concentration. “My toes are here,” she announced, with great wonder, as though she had found them for the first time in her life. It was a very small discovery, and yet it was the very same one that had once surprised a grown woman in a cold hall.

After a while Nia said, in a small thoughtful voice, that her worry felt like a little cloud sitting in her tummy. Maya, hiding a smile that was mostly tears, told her that clouds always pass and that the big blue sky is still there behind every one of them. Nia considered this seriously, nodded and said that she thought her cloud was getting smaller.

Within ten minutes Nia was fast asleep, with her rabbit tucked beneath her chin and one hand flung out across the pillow, and the whole small room was filled with the sound of her slow breathing. Maya sat in the quiet on the edge of the bed, listening to the clock in the hall and the soft rain on the window. She was not waiting for anything, and she was not anywhere else but here.

Later Maya sat alone at the kitchen table with a mug of tea and the pebble resting beside it, and let her mind travel back over the weeks since that first burnt and breathless Monday. Her life had not been rearranged, her problems were all still in their places and her sister's early shifts and her manager's folders were just as they had been. And yet, for the first time in years, she felt at home inside it.

Maya counted the ideas on her fingers, one by one, as one counts the stones in a path. The breath is an anchor, because it is always here and always now, and the pause is a small space in which we can choose, and our feelings are weather, which arrives and changes and passes while the sky remains. Most precious of all, she thought, was the quiet permission to begin again, as often as she needed.

She remembered, too, what Mrs Adeyemi had always said honestly, which was that mindfulness is a skill and a companion and not a cure, and that it helps many people but not everyone. Anyone who feels very low or anxious for a long time should speak to a doctor or to someone they trust, and there is no shame in doing so, any more than in asking for directions. Asking for help, Maya thought, is one more way of being awake to our own lives.

That is all the practice asks of you: to be here, to breathe, to notice what is happening without judgment, and to begin again as often as you need. Mindfulness is a skill and a companion, not a cure, and it can be practised on a bus, in a queue, at a kitchen table or on the edge of a child's bed. This book offers general information only, and it is not medical advice, so it can never take the place of a conversation with a professional who knows you.
